observations:
LM2 Torah #109 is a three-sentence teaching of exceptional brevity. It introduces one clear conceptual domain — the Eretz Yisrael / burial-place-of-the-tzaddik identity (Package 1) — and one eitza relationship pointing outward from that domain (Eretz Yisrael repairs the blemish of the Brit).

The question of whether a second independent package exists was examined carefully:

1. COULD 'פגם הברית' (blemish of the Brit) form its own package? No. It appears once, in a single sentence, as the target of an eitza. There are no bechina connections linking פגם הברית to any other concept in this Torah. A package requires bechina-connected nodes; a single isolated concept referenced only as an eitza target does not qualify. It would need at least two concepts explicitly connected by bechina language (sharing the same essential nature) to form even a minimal package.

2. COULD the Baal Shem Tov's grave (mentioned in the opening sentence) form a sub-package? No. The opening sentence is context-setting narrative ('He spoke with me about the matter of the grave of the Baal Shem Tov, that it is very good to be there at his grave'). This introduces the topic but does not use bechina language. The grave of the Besht is an exemplar of the principle stated in sentence 2 — it is the burial place of a true tzaddik, and thus falls under the מקום גניזה node of Package 1. It does not constitute a separate conceptual domain.

3. COULD 'ירושה' (inheritance) form its own package? No. The Rebbe uses the inheritance language from Psalms 37:29 ('צַדִּיקִים יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ') as an exegetical vehicle to teach the bechina of burial place = Eretz Yisrael. Inheritance here is the mode of acquisition, not an independent domain with bechina partners.

4. COULD the good/evil mirror structure require an evil package? Normally the framework expects evil mirrors for good packages. Here, פגם הברית is named as the evil/negative reality that Package 1 (Eretz Yisrael) repairs. However, פגם הברית in this Torah has no bechina partners — it appears once as an eitza target. Its evil domain is acknowledged but cannot be formalized as a package without at least two bechina-connected nodes.

Conclusion: The single package identified — אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמְקוֹם גְּנִיזַת הַצַּדִּיק — fully exhausts the bechina-connected conceptual structure of this Torah. The teaching is a sharp, minimal statement: the true tzaddik inherits Eretz Yisrael (in the sense that his burial place IS Eretz Yisrael in holiness), and Eretz Yisrael repairs the blemish of the Brit. There is one bechina (burial place ↔ Eretz Yisrael) and one eitza (Eretz Yisrael → tikkun for brit-blemish). No additional independent domain with 3+ bechina-connected concepts exists in the text.
